abstract: In this issue's cover feature, Tim J Wright discusses the earthquake deformation cycle and seismic hazard in the continents – the 2015 Bullerwell Lecture.

In 1914, the RAS recognized as an Honorary Member Annie Jump Cannon, whose prodigious analysis of spectra led her to develop today's robust stellar classification, writes Sue Bowler.

abstract: Astronomy won't make you blind, according to Thomas Hockey, but there were and are sightless stargazers, not counting the character in the movie Contact.

Ciarán D Beggan and Steve R Marple describe how they are using low-cost computers to develop a network of school magnetometers for measuring space-weather effects in the UK.

Caroline Herschel escaped domestic drudgery for a singing career, yet found satisfaction and success through astronomy, both assisting her brother William and nephew John and in her own right. Michael Hoskin surveys her life and achievements.

articleTitle: Star formation in the Gaia era
abstract: The kinematics of stars is fundamental to understanding how they formed. Nicholas Wright reports on an RAS Specialist Discussion Meeting that focused on how Gaia's star-mapping data will revolutionize our view of stellar dynamics.
Julia Wilkinson and a Zooniverse citizen-science team examine Arctic auroral data, using observations from the ill-fated 19th-century Arctic exploration ship USS Jeannette.
Ian Crawford, Martin Elvis and James Carpenter summarize an RAS Specialist Discussion Meeting which examined how science will benefit from the use of extraterrestrial resources.

The Square Kilometre Array needs industrial expertise; SKA technology will, in turn, streamline big-data challenges for business and society. Or that's the idea: Sue Bowler reports on a day of networking designed to build industry–academia collaborations in the UK.

Charlie Walker, Ben Shaw and colleagues give an overview of how the sensitivity, superb resolution and lack of obscuration in e-MERLIN data is changing what we know about our home galaxy and the lifecycles of its stars.
Tom Muxlow and colleagues round up the potential of e-MERLIN for examining the large-scale structure and evolution of the universe.

articleTitle: Mapping limits to life on Earth
abstract: Kenneth Freeman and colleagues take a look at extremophiles and ask how their biology fits them for life on and off planet Earth.

abstract: In January 1916, the RAS elected its first women Fellows. Mandy Bailey looks back at the social and scientific circumstances of this step towards equality, introducing a year of articles celebrating the centenary.

abstract: Ignacio Ferreras, Francesco La Barbera and Alexandre Vazdekis take a close look at one of the key ingredients in modelling star formation.

articleTitle: The lunar highlands: old crust, new ideas
abstract: John Pernet-Fisher and Katherine Joy describe how our understanding of lunar crustal formation has evolved over the past few decades.
Don Kurtz, Simon Jeffrey and Conny Aerts describe discoveries in the new era of precision asteroseismology.
John Coxon and colleagues sum up a Magnetosphere, Ionosphere and Solar–Terrestrial meeting that touched on topics across the solar system.

Deep in the heart of the Cheshire countryside lies Jodrell Bank Observatory, home to the UK's national facility for high-resolution radio astronomy: e-MERLIN, the enhanced Multi-Element Remote-Linked Interferometer Network. In this issue of A&G, the e-MERLIN team highlights some of its cutting-edge experiments, probing fundamental physical processes in our own galaxy, and reaching further out to higher redshift where radio astronomy can investigate cosmic history and evolution. In this first article, Simon Garrington and Rob Beswick explain how e-MERLIN came to be.
Megan Argo and colleagues discuss what can be determined from galactic observations and surveys using e-MERLIN.

articleTitle: Margaret Huggins and Tulse Hill Observatory
abstract: Photography, instrument design, methodology, interpretation – all skills brought to William Huggins' observatory by his persistent and careful wife Margaret. Together they developed spectroscopy into a powerful research tool. Barbara Becker tells the story.

articleTitle: Space to Earth Challenge takes off in UK schools
abstract: Helen Mason and Heather MacRae think Principia has succeeded in energizing kids' interest in space, and explain how schools and individuals can still get involved.
Shannon Bohle, H Saul Perez Montaño, Matt Bille and Doug Turnbull consider what it might take to grow plants on Mars, in this issue's cover feature.
